narrative.text: The cataloguing and copyright page of the Portuguese edition of the 2012 WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, with ISBNs for both organizations and standard disclaimers.

The foreword by the heads of WHO and the International Telecommunication Union, presenting the toolkit as a major joint effort to help countries at all levels of development use ICT for health. It stresses national eHealth strategies as a route to lasting gains in public and individual health.
Thanks the steering committee, technical advisers, Deloitte consultants, editors and country and partner reviewers who contributed to the first edition of the toolkit.
The table of contents, listing the foreword, acknowledgements, introduction and the toolkit's three parts on vision, action plan and monitoring and evaluation.
A section title page for the introduction to the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit.

Describes what the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit is and who it is for: a framework and method for any government developing or renewing a national eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework. It explains the toolkit's three parts and how they build on each other, and that it draws on the experience of countries with existing strategies. It notes that it is aimed at senior health and ICT officials but keeps the general public, as ultimate beneficiaries, in mind.
A title page for Part 1 of the toolkit, on the national eHealth vision.
The title page and repeated cataloguing and copyright information for Part 1 of the toolkit, on establishing a national eHealth vision.

Explains the purpose of Part 1, noting that it suits countries just starting with eHealth and those scaling up pilots or updating strategies. It outlines the structure of the chapters and annexes, including definitions of common terms.
The table of contents for Part 1, listing twelve chapters from the national context for eHealth to refining the vision and strategic recommendations, plus annexes, figures and tables.

Sets out the national context for eHealth, defining it as the use of ICT for health and describing how it is changing health care delivery and responsive health systems. It explains why a national approach is needed given constrained budgets, workforce shortages and growing demands, and how eHealth fits into health systems and services. The chapter covers the building blocks of a national eHealth environment, such as leadership and governance, services and applications, infrastructure, standards, legislation and workforce. It ends by introducing the framework for a national eHealth vision in the next chapter.

Presents the framework for a national eHealth vision, which explains why a national approach is needed, what it will achieve and how. It describes the strategic context, eHealth outcomes and required components, and points to a suggested structure for the vision document in an annex.

Gives an overview of the method for developing a national eHealth vision, based on experience from countries that already have strategies. It describes an iterative approach: drafting an unconstrained vision, then refining it against the current eHealth environment, opportunities and gaps. The final phase produces strategic recommendations that feed Part 2, along with approval and communication of the vision.

Covers managing the process of developing the eHealth vision, with sections on health sector leadership, governance structures, the core strategy team and timelines and milestones. It explains how a respected leader or leadership team secures resources and signals sector ownership, and gives an example governance model with roles. It lists the skills the team needs and shows sample timelines for completing the work.

Describes engaging stakeholders in developing the eHealth vision, starting with clarifying the government's role and identifying stakeholder groups inside and outside the health sector. It explains how to understand stakeholder roles, influence and interests and how to choose suitable engagement approaches linked to a communication plan. Sample tables show a consultation plan and consultation methods, such as interviews, small group forums and teleconferences. The chapter stresses minimizing repeated consultations with the same people.

Explains establishing the strategic context for the eHealth vision by researching population health and demographics, describing the health system and identifying the national health strategy. It provides tables of questions on population, health outcomes, service delivery, workforce and financing, with recommended outputs and methods. Further steps cover non-health drivers such as development goals and regional commitments, and selecting the goals and challenges eHealth can best address. The chapter ends by describing how eHealth and improved health information flows can support these goals in and beyond the health sector.

Describes learning from other countries' eHealth experience, both successes and failures, and from international trends and best practice. It sets out research into other national eHealth visions, strategies and programmes, supplemented by exploratory interviews or study tours. It names sources such as government, agency and industry reports, academic publications and WHO.

Covers drafting an initial unconstrained eHealth vision, starting with agreeing the time horizon and defining the eHealth outcomes sought through sample questions. It describes linking outcomes to the strategic context, writing a high-level vision statement and setting out benefits for each stakeholder group. Examples include a sample vision for health care providers and a scenario showing how eHealth would change a patient's experience. The chapter ends by advising that scenarios be reviewed with stakeholder groups to build accuracy and support.

Describes identifying the eHealth components, or building blocks, needed to deliver the draft vision, starting with leadership and governance and strategy and investment. Tables give examples of components, such as programme management, stakeholder engagement, strategic architecture and funding. Further sections cover services and applications, infrastructure, standards and interoperability, legislation and policy, and the eHealth workforce. The chapter ends with developing non-technical architecture models of the components, citing an Australian national eHealth strategy as a source.

Chapter 10 of the Portuguese edition of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, on gathering information about a country's current eHealth environment. It sets out the aim of describing existing or planned eHealth components to find opportunities for reuse and gaps to fill. It gives example questions under seven component areas: leadership and governance, strategy and investment, services and applications, infrastructure, standards and interoperability, legislation and policy, and workforce. It ends by suggesting whom to consult, urging a broad view that includes e-government components, and warning against spending too much time on this step.

Chapter 11 of the eHealth strategy toolkit (in Portuguese), on assessing opportunities, gaps, risks and barriers by comparing required eHealth components with those already in place. It describes the outputs, namely components that can be reused, those that must be developed and associated risks, illustrated by a figure. It notes that a stakeholder reference group can identify whom to consult.

Chapter 12 of the eHealth strategy toolkit (in Portuguese), on refining the initial vision into an ambitious but pragmatic national eHealth vision and developing strategic recommendations. It covers adjusting scope and priorities using internal and external factors, shown in a table. It explains how recommendations are drafted to implement the required components. It ends with obtaining approval from decision-makers and communicating the vision through a period of public awareness and consultation.

Annex A of the toolkit (in Portuguese), giving examples of eHealth drawn from the WHO Global Observatory for eHealth. It defines electronic medical records, electronic health records and personal health records. It describes telemedicine services such as store-and-forward teleradiology and other applications including health information systems, citing the Health Metrics Network framework.

Annex B of the toolkit (in Portuguese), a table of example eHealth benefits in areas such as access to services, efficiency, quality and safety of care, health monitoring, access to knowledge, planning, citizen empowerment and innovation, with sources.
Annex C of the toolkit (in Portuguese), giving a suggested structure for a national eHealth vision document, from strategic context and vision to foundations for change and strategic recommendations.

Annex D of the toolkit (in Portuguese), a table summarising the method for developing a national eHealth vision, with the activities and outputs of each phase. Phases include gathering information on the current environment across the seven component areas, assessing opportunities and gaps, and refining the vision and recommendations. Outputs include an approved vision and its communication to stakeholders.

Annex E of the toolkit (in Portuguese), an example map of national eHealth components that can be used to identify and assess components. It covers leadership and governance, strategy and investment, services and applications such as electronic records and referrals, infrastructure, standards and interoperability, and workforce skills.

Annex F of the toolkit (in Portuguese), describing a governance continuum for a national eHealth vision, from a fully regulated centralized bureaucratic model to a free-market model. It explains the guided-market model in between, which combines central coordination in areas of national importance with flexibility elsewhere.

Annex G of the toolkit (in Portuguese), defining terms used in Part 1, such as strategic goals and challenges, eHealth outcomes, eHealth vision, national eHealth environment, eHealth components and strategic recommendations. It also defines output and outcome indicators.
A divider fragment with the words 'National eHealth Strategy' (in Portuguese).

The title and cataloguing page of Part 2 of the toolkit (in Portuguese), on developing a national eHealth action plan, with WHO and ITU ISBNs, 2012 copyright, ordering and permissions information and disclaimers.

Introduces Part 2 of the toolkit (in Portuguese), which builds on the national eHealth vision from Part 1 to develop a comprehensive action plan suited to each country's circumstances and priorities. It describes the plan as a widely published document for stakeholders and explains the intended audience of government health leaders. It outlines how the chapters and annexes are organized.

The table of contents of Part 2 of the toolkit (in Portuguese), listing chapters on the action plan framework, managing the process, engaging stakeholders, action lines, integrated planning, resources, funding constraints and implementation periods. It also lists the annexes, figures, boxes and tables, such as examples of activities, risks and public–private partnerships.

Introduces the move from vision to action plan (in Portuguese): Part 1 sets out why eHealth is needed and what it will deliver, while Part 2 describes how the vision will be achieved through action lines and resources.

Chapter 1 of Part 2 (in Portuguese), setting out the framework for an eHealth action plan built on action lines, resources and strategic phases. It explains that grouping activities into action lines and time-bound phases makes planning and funding more practical, and refers to a suggested plan structure in Annex A.

Chapter 2 of Part 2 (in Portuguese), giving an overview of the iterative method for developing a national eHealth action plan. It summarises each step, including managing the process, engaging stakeholders, developing action lines, building an integrated plan, estimating resources, applying funding constraints and defining implementation periods.

Chapter 3 of Part 2 (in Portuguese), on managing the development of the eHealth action plan. It covers sustaining ministerial and health sector leadership, adapting governance structures from Part 1, ensuring a core team with the right skills, and setting a timetable. Example timelines for the planning steps are shown in a figure.

Chapter 4 of Part 2 (in Portuguese), on engaging stakeholders in developing the eHealth action plan. It explains how the government's role, from fully regulated to free market, shapes the level of stakeholder involvement, as shown in a table. It covers identifying stakeholder groups, choosing a pragmatic approach based on influence and expertise, and planning consultations. It ends with a table of stakeholder roles at each planning step, such as advising on skills, costs and likely funding and approving the refined plan.

Chapter 5 of Part 2 of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, in Portuguese, explains how to develop individual plans for each eHealth action line as the first step in building a national eHealth action plan. It describes grouping the activities needed to realize the national eHealth vision into action lines such as governance, foundations, solutions, and change and adoption, and what each delivers. It sets out an approach that combines internal analysis with stakeholder input to refine or extend the action lines. It also covers setting out activities, outputs, dependencies and risks for each line, with stakeholder consultation where refinement is needed.

Chapter 6, in Portuguese, describes combining the individual action line plans into one integrated eHealth action plan for the national vision. It shows how activities across governance, standards, infrastructure and solutions fit together and how dependencies and remaining risks should be identified and managed. It explains checking that the plan aligns with health system priorities and stakeholder expectations, and adjusting it to the preferred options agreed with stakeholders.

Chapter 7, in Portuguese, covers estimating at a high level the resources, skills and experience needed to carry out the eHealth action plan. It describes assessing resource type, scale and distribution, and comparing needs with what exists in the country through questions on available people, skills, locations and existing programmes. It advises presenting cost estimates as ranges with clearly stated assumptions so decision makers do not mistake them for exact figures.

Chapter 8, in Portuguese, explains how to refine the eHealth action plan in line with the country's funding constraints. It describes identifying potential funding sources, the timeframe over which funds are available and the conditions attached, such as donor links to health outcomes. It covers assessing options and their impact and updating the national eHealth vision to reflect the preferred option.

Chapter 9, in Portuguese, explains how to define implementation periods that make the complex eHealth action plan easy to communicate, each with targets for developing and using eHealth. It describes setting a strategic focus for each period, moving from establishing basic communication to wider information sharing and finally to consolidating eHealth as routine care. It also lists questions for describing each period's outcomes and impact on stakeholders.

Annex A, in Portuguese, proposes a structure and table of contents for a national eHealth action plan, stressing that the document should be accessible to a wide audience as well as those who will implement it.

Annex B, in Portuguese, summarizes the methodology for developing a national eHealth action plan in a table listing each phase, its activities and its outputs, from managing the process through to defining implementation periods and targets.

Annex C, in Portuguese, maps the components of the national eHealth landscape from Part 1 of the toolkit onto the action lines of Chapter 5, such as governance, foundations, solutions and change and adoption, in a two-page figure. Components include leadership and governance, services and applications, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, legislation and workforce.

Annex D, in Portuguese, gives examples of possible activities under each of the four common eHealth action lines, stressing that the list is illustrative rather than complete. Governance activities include setting up and formalizing eHealth governance bodies alongside existing national, regional and local structures. Foundation activities cover designing, installing and managing core eHealth services and defining processes for national standards. Solution and adoption activities include exploring specific issues and risks in developing the national eHealth environment.

Annex E, in Portuguese, gives non-exhaustive examples of risks linked to eHealth action plan activities, grouped by area such as leadership and governance, with tables describing each risk type. Examples include lack of credible senior leaders and dependence on vendor products that may not be available when needed. The annex aims to show common risk areas that should be explored rather than list every risk.

Annex F, in Portuguese, explains public–private partnerships, defined as arrangements in which the private sector helps design, plan, finance, build or manage projects normally run by the public sector. It lists reasons governments use them, such as value for money, risk sharing and budget limits, and their challenges. It notes other ways of involving the private sector in eHealth, such as subcontracting.
Annex G, in Portuguese, defines terms used in the toolkit, organized by part, such as strategic goals and challenges, eHealth outcomes and outcome indicators.
A heading fragment carrying the toolkit's title, 'National eHealth Strategy'.

Opens Part 3 of the toolkit, on monitoring and evaluation, in Portuguese, with the cataloguing data, ISBNs for WHO and ITU and the 2012 copyright notice. It introduces the part's purpose, assessing progress and results of a national eHealth strategy, and outlines its chapters on building a monitoring and evaluation framework and the supporting annexes.

The table of contents of Part 3, in Portuguese, listing chapters on the eHealth monitoring and evaluation framework, indicators, baselines and targets, governance and processes, annexes on results-based management and example strategies, and lists of figures.

Introduces Part 3 of the Portuguese edition of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, on monitoring and evaluating progress and results. It recalls that by this stage a country should have an approved eHealth vision and action plan describing action lines, outputs, dependencies, resources and timing. It explains that a monitoring and evaluation framework, based on results-based management, lets governments track outcomes, and points to an annex for more detail.

Describes the elements of an eHealth monitoring and evaluation framework: meaningful indicators of adoption, use and outcomes, baseline and target measures, and governance with supporting processes. It stresses that governance provides oversight and timely intervention when progress diverges from plans.

Gives an overview of developing an eHealth monitoring and evaluation framework as a sequence: defining indicators, setting baseline and target values, and defining governance and supporting processes. It notes that targets allow actual progress to be compared with planned progress and that monitoring at various levels should fit one national model.

Covers the first step of the eHealth monitoring framework, defining output and outcome indicators linked to the stakeholders and outcomes identified in Part 1. It sets out activities such as identifying priority stakeholders, analysing eHealth outcomes for them and selecting indicators of adoption and outcomes. It provides example indicators across eHealth components and guidance on choosing measurable ones. It closes by recommending a mix of quantitative and qualitative measures and the skills to use both.

Explains how to set baseline and target values for each eHealth indicator and a timetable for comparing them, so progress against the action plan can be judged. It describes how baselines show a country's starting point and help set realistic targets. It covers sources of baseline data, how to estimate targets from expected adoption and its effects on service delivery and patients. It advises reviewing proposed indicators and targets with experts and stakeholders.

Describes how to define national governance and processes for monitoring and evaluating the eHealth action plan. It outlines a governance model with roles for a steering committee and other bodies at different levels. It sets out a high-level process for collecting, analysing and reporting indicator data. It ends with steps for reviewing and revising unrealistic targets, approved by the programme steering committee.

Concludes the eHealth toolkit by noting that its vision, action plan and monitoring framework reflect a point in time and must be updated as a country's strategic context changes. It stresses continued stakeholder engagement and regular communication on progress to maintain transparency and support.

An annex explaining results-based management, increasingly used by UN agencies, which shifts focus from processes to performance, outcomes and impacts. It describes the results chain and how programmes using it concentrate resources on expected results. It also outlines steps for planning and carrying out evaluation, from data sources to recommendations and lessons learned.

An annex listing examples of national and state eHealth strategies and roadmaps that countries such as Australia, Denmark, Switzerland and the United States have published online, with links and dates, noting that they predate the toolkit.

An annex defining terms used in each part of the eHealth toolkit, such as strategic goals and challenges, eHealth outcomes and eHealth vision. It describes how improved information flows and electronic access change health services. It ends with the back cover text describing the toolkit as a major WHO–ITU collaboration, with ISBN.
